stem: A design team wants a structured way to enumerate threats such as spoofing, tampering, and information disclosure against a new application. Which threat modeling methodology BEST fits?

options.rationale: STRIDE categorizes threats as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege — exactly the enumeration described.
RAID refers to redundant disk arrays, not a threat modeling methodology.
OSI is a networking reference model, not a threat modeling framework.
COBIT is an IT governance framework, not a per-threat enumeration model.

stem: In STRIDE, a user performs a harmful transaction and later denies doing it, and the system lacks reliable logs. This maps MOST directly to which STRIDE category, and which property does it violate?

options.rationale: The inability to prove who performed an action is the Repudiation threat, which undermines the non-repudiation property.
Spoofing is impersonation and maps to authentication, not to denying one's own action.
Tampering is unauthorized modification affecting integrity, not the denial of an action.
DoS affects availability by disrupting service, unrelated to denying an action was performed.

stem: After threat modeling reveals many exposed, unused services on a server, what is the BEST mitigation?

options.text: Reduce the attack surface by disabling/removing unnecessary services and interfaces
options.rationale: Removing unneeded services and interfaces directly reduces the attack surface exposed to threats.

options.text: Add more unused services for redundancy
options.rationale: Adding more services increases, not reduces, the attack surface.

options.text: Publish the full service list publicly
options.rationale: Publishing exposed services aids attackers and does not mitigate risk.

options.text: Ignore the finding since it is only theoretical
options.rationale: Unused exposed services are real, exploitable exposure, not merely theoretical.

stem: A team begins threat modeling a system. To understand where threats could arise, what should they typically create FIRST?

options.text: A data flow diagram identifying components, data flows, and trust boundaries
options.rationale: Mapping the system with a DFD (components, flows, trust boundaries) is the foundational first step that reveals where threats can occur.
Marketing plans are irrelevant to identifying technical threats.
A pen test occurs later against a built system; it cannot precede design-stage modeling.
Staff scheduling has nothing to do with mapping system threats.

stem: In a data flow diagram, where should a threat modeler MOST focus attention for potential attacks?

options.text: At trust boundaries where data crosses between components of differing trust levels
options.rationale: Trust boundaries — where data moves between differently-trusted zones — are the highest-value focus for identifying threats like tampering and spoofing.

options.text: Only on the application's color scheme
options.rationale: Visual styling is irrelevant to threat analysis.

options.text: Only inside a single trusted component where no data crosses
options.rationale: Threats concentrate where trust levels change; a single fully-trusted internal component is lower priority.

options.text: On the physical weight of the server hardware
options.rationale: Hardware weight has no relevance to threat modeling.

stem: PASTA is a threat modeling methodology characterized by which of the following?

options.text: A risk-centric, seven-stage process aligning threats to business objectives
options.rationale: PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) is a seven-stage, risk-centric methodology that ties technical threats to business impact.
PASTA is not a storage/RAID standard.
PASTA is a threat modeling process, not a password policy.
PASTA has nothing to do with wireless encryption.

stem: To make threat models reflect real-world adversaries, what input is BEST incorporated?

options.text: Current threat intelligence about relevant adversaries and their tactics
options.rationale: Feeding real threat intelligence (adversary TTPs) grounds the model in realistic, current threats rather than guesswork.
Financial dividend data is irrelevant to modeling adversary behavior.
Personal preferences do not inform realistic threat modeling.
Operational trivia has no bearing on adversary modeling.

stem: When is threat modeling MOST cost-effective to perform in the system development lifecycle?

options.text: Early, during design, so issues are addressed before they are built and costly to fix
options.rationale: Identifying threats at design time is far cheaper than remediating them after implementation or in production.

options.text: Only after the system is fully deployed to production
options.rationale: Post-deployment fixes are the most expensive and disruptive; modeling should start earlier.

options.text: Only after a breach has already occurred
options.rationale: Waiting for a breach is reactive and defeats the preventive value of modeling.

options.text: Never, since design will change anyway
options.rationale: Design evolution is a reason to model iteratively, not to skip modeling entirely.

stem: After enumerating threats, a team wants to rank them by factors like damage, reproducibility, and affected users. Which model BEST supports this ranking?

options.rationale: DREAD scores threats by Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, and Discoverability to prioritize them.
STRIDE categorizes threat types but is not primarily a numeric prioritization/ranking scheme.
RAID is a disk redundancy scheme, unrelated to threat ranking.
ZAP is a scanning tool, not a threat prioritization model.

stem: An analyst wants to model the various paths an attacker could take to reach a goal, with the goal at the root and methods as branches. This technique is MOST accurately called what?

options.rationale: An attack tree places the attacker's goal at the root and decomposes possible attack paths as branches/subgoals.
A Gantt chart schedules project tasks over time, unrelated to attack paths.
An org chart shows reporting structure, not attack methods.
A cabling diagram shows physical wiring, not adversary attack paths.

stem: A low-privileged user exploits a flaw to gain administrative rights. In STRIDE, this maps MOST directly to which category?

options.rationale: Gaining higher privileges than authorized is the Elevation of Privilege threat in STRIDE.
Information Disclosure is unauthorized data exposure, not gaining elevated rights.
DoS disrupts availability; it does not describe privilege gain.
Spoofing is impersonating another identity, distinct from escalating one's own privileges.

stem: In STRIDE, the 'Tampering' threat most directly threatens which security property?

options.rationale: Tampering is unauthorized modification of data or code, which directly threatens integrity.
Availability is threatened by Denial of Service, not by tampering specifically.
Authentication is threatened by Spoofing, not by tampering.
Non-repudiation is threatened by Repudiation, not by tampering.

stem: For threat modeling to be effective on a software project, who should BEST be involved?

options.text: A cross-functional group including developers, architects, and security personnel
options.rationale: Effective threat modeling needs diverse perspectives — those who design, build, and secure the system — to surface realistic threats.
Marketing lacks the technical/security knowledge to identify system threats.

options.text: A single junior developer working alone
options.rationale: One person in isolation is likely to miss threats a cross-functional review would catch.
Customers cannot analyze internal design and trust boundaries.

stem: During threat modeling, a large complex system is broken into smaller components to analyze each more thoroughly. This decomposition step is MOST accurately known as what?

options.rationale: Reduction analysis decomposes the system into manageable components/data flows so threats can be examined systematically at each part.
Risk acceptance is a treatment decision, not a decomposition activity.
Pen testing actively probes a built system; it is not the analytic decomposition of a model.
A BIA assesses impact of lost functions, not the structural decomposition for threat analysis.

stem: A high-severity spoofing threat is identified. Which mitigation BEST addresses it?

options.text: Strong authentication (e.g., MFA, mutual TLS) to verify identities
options.rationale: Spoofing (impersonation) is countered by robust authentication that reliably verifies the identity of parties.

options.text: Increasing screen brightness on the server
options.rationale: This has no security effect on spoofing.
Removing logging reduces detection capability and does nothing to prevent spoofing.
Broadening access increases exposure and does not counter identity spoofing.

stem: A modeler distinguishes core terms. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: A threat is a potential cause of harm, a vulnerability is a weakness it can exploit, and risk is the likelihood and impact of that occurring
options.rationale: This correctly separates threat (potential danger), vulnerability (exploitable weakness), and risk (likelihood × impact of exploitation).

options.text: Threat, vulnerability, and risk are identical terms
options.rationale: They are distinct concepts; conflating them is a common error.

options.text: A vulnerability is an attacker and a threat is a patch
options.rationale: These definitions are wrong; a vulnerability is a weakness, not an attacker.

options.text: Risk exists only after a breach happens
options.rationale: Risk is a forward-looking likelihood/impact measure that exists before any breach.

stem: An API accidentally returns other users' records in responses. In STRIDE, this is MOST directly which category?

options.rationale: Exposing data to parties not authorized to see it is the Information Disclosure threat, undermining confidentiality.
No privilege escalation is described; data is simply being disclosed improperly.
The service is functioning (over-returning data), so this is not a DoS.
Repudiation concerns denying actions; it does not describe leaking others' data.

stem: After applying mitigations, some threats cannot be fully eliminated within budget. What is the BEST way to handle these remaining threats?

options.text: Document them, assess residual risk, and obtain a risk-acceptance decision from an appropriate authority
options.rationale: Threats that can't be fully mitigated should be documented with residual risk assessed and formally accepted by an authorized owner.

options.text: Delete the threat model so they are not visible
options.rationale: Hiding the analysis does not remove the risk and undermines accountability.

options.text: Assume they will never be exploited
options.rationale: Unfounded assumptions of non-exploitation are not a valid treatment.

options.text: Grant attackers access to test them
options.rationale: Deliberately exposing the system to attackers is reckless, not a treatment.

stem: How do STRIDE and DREAD MOST accurately relate in a threat modeling process?

options.text: STRIDE helps identify/categorize threats; DREAD helps rate/prioritize them
options.rationale: STRIDE is for enumerating threat types while DREAD scores/prioritizes identified threats — they serve complementary stages.

options.text: They are competing tools that cannot be used together
options.rationale: They are complementary and are frequently used together.
Neither is an encryption algorithm; both are threat modeling aids.

options.text: DREAD identifies threats and STRIDE ranks them
options.rationale: This reverses their roles; STRIDE identifies, DREAD ranks.

stem: What is the PRIMARY value of the output produced by a threat modeling exercise?

options.text: It drives prioritized security requirements and controls to mitigate the most significant threats
options.rationale: The core value is translating identified threats into prioritized, actionable security requirements and mitigations.

options.text: It replaces the need for any coding standards
options.rationale: Threat modeling complements, not replaces, secure coding standards.

options.text: It guarantees the product will have zero vulnerabilities
options.rationale: No exercise guarantees zero vulnerabilities; it reduces and prioritizes risk.

options.text: It serves mainly as a marketing document
options.rationale: Threat models are technical security artifacts, not marketing collateral.
